assumptions: That the alert itself was genuine is assumed, not verified — with no metrics, we cannot rule out a false positive or a fault in the alerting pipeline.
The reported duration is treated as unreliable rather than as evidence of a brief outage; a near-zero interval most likely reflects how the incident record was closed.
Customer impact is unknown in both directions: we are not claiming there was none, only that we have no evidence either way.
No remediation is claimed for io-shop, since no cause was found; if the error rate was real and has since subsided, the reason is unknown.
input.executive_summary:
An automated monitor reported an elevated error rate on one internal service. The automated investigation that follows such an alert was unable to retrieve any of the measurements it needs, and so it handed the incident to people without a conclusion. No corrective action was taken, because nothing was identified to correct.

We do not know what, if anything, customers experienced. We cannot state how long the condition lasted: the alert's recorded start and end are essentially the same instant, which is more consistent with the alert being closed out when the investigation failed than with a real problem that resolved itself immediately. Because the underlying data could not be read, we also cannot confirm that any errors actually occurred.

The concrete follow-up is not about the service that alerted but about the monitoring path: we need to find out why no measurements were available, so that the next alert of this kind can be investigated rather than abandoned.
input.root_cause: Not determined. An automated HighErrorRate alert fired on io-shop, but no metrics could be retrieved for the incident window, so the investigation was escalated with no cause identified and no candidate hypothesis was ever tested. The only firm finding is a gap in our ability to read metrics for this service at the time of the alert — which may itself be the reason the alert appeared, or may be independent of it.
